js_003: Who left behind The Baekbeom Diary as a leader of Korea’s Provisional Government?
js_005: Choe Nam-seon, who drafted the Declaration of Independence
js_006: Ahn Chang-ho, who founded the Young Korean Academy
js_007: Sin Chae-ho, who wrote History of Ancient Joseon
js_008: It’s the memoir Kim Gu (1876–1949) wrote to leave for his two sons. His pen name was Baekbeom; his childhood name was Changam, later changed to Changsu, and finally to Gu.
js_010: What kind of writing is The Baekbeom Diary?
js_011: A memoir Kim Gu wrote to leave for his two sons
js_012: A record of Kim Gu’s sayings, taken down by his students
js_013: A prison diary Kim Gu kept day by day
js_014: An official activity report published by the Provisional Government
js_015: He began writing it as a will for his sons In and Sin, not knowing when he might die. That’s why it includes as many of his own faults as things to be proud of.
js_017: What meaning did Kim Gu pack into the pen name he chose for himself, “Baekbeom”?
js_018: That everyone, from the lowliest outcast to the most ordinary person, would hold love of country
js_019: That he’d live out his life as an ordinary scholar in white clothes, like any commoner
js_020: A vow to rise again a hundred times, however many times he fell
js_021: A state of mind drawn from walking alone across a snow-covered field
js_022: He drew from baekjeong (the lowest outcast class) and beombu (an ordinary person). Packed into these two characters is the belief that even the most despised people should become masters of their nation.
js_024: What organization did Kim Gu join at eighteen and rise to local leader of the following year?
js_025: A Christian youth association founded by Western missionaries
js_026: Byeolgigun, a modernized army King Gojong created
js_027: The People’s Joint Association, led by the Independence Club
js_028: In 1893, at eighteen, he joined Donghak and became a local leader the following year. Its teaching that even outcasts deserved to be treated as human moved a boy who kept running into the wall of class.
js_030: What cause did Kim Gu cite for killing a Japanese man at Chihapo in 1896?
js_032: Reclaiming grain that had been seized
js_034: Carrying out a secret royal order
js_035: It came the year after Empress Myeongseong was assassinated in the Eulmi Incident. Kim Gu stated it plainly as avenging the queen.
js_037: How did Kim Gu, jailed for the Chihapo incident, escape execution?
js_038: The king ultimately never approved the death sentence
js_039: A Japanese consul asked for leniency and he was released at once
js_040: Fellow inmates took the blame in his place
js_041: He was retried and found not guilty
js_042: The Justice Ministry sent up an order for hanging, but King Gojong never approved it, so it was never carried out. The Baekbeom Diary describes the royal order as having arrived by telephone, though historians note this doesn’t match when phone service actually began.
js_044: Which temple did the escaped Kim Gu hide out in as a monk, and what dharma name did he receive?
js_045: He received the dharma name Wonjong at Magoksa
js_046: He received the dharma name Wonmyeong at Yujeomsa
js_047: He received the dharma name Manhae at Haeinsa
js_048: He received the dharma name Gyeongheo at Tongdosa
js_049: He shaved his head at Magoksa in Gongju, Chungcheong Province, and received the dharma name Wonjong. His life as a monk didn’t last long — he returned to lay life the following year.
js_051: What was the first post Kim Gu held after fleeing to Shanghai in 1919 to join the Provisional Government?
js_056: He served as Chief of Police, the government’s security arm, weeding out spies and turncoats. He later rose through Head of State to President.
js_058: What was the name of the direct-action organization Kim Gu founded in 1931?
js_060: The Righteous Corps, led by Kim Won-bong
js_063: Kim Gu personally founded the Korean Patriotic Corps to revive a Provisional Government that had lost momentum. Both Yi Bong-chang and Yun Bong-gil were members.
js_065: Which Korean Patriotic Corps member threw a bomb in Hongkou Park, Shanghai, in 1932?
js_066: Na Seok-ju, who attacked the Oriental Development Company
js_069: On April 29, 1932, Yun Bong-gil threw a bomb onto the stage of a ceremony marking the emperor’s birthday and the fall of Shanghai. This act dramatically changed the Provisional Government’s standing.

js_091: His childhood name was Changam, later changed to Changsu, then to Gu while in prison. The name Gu (龜, “turtle”) and the pen name Yeonha were given to him by his teacher-like mentor, Yu In-mu.
js_092: The “diary” in the title isn’t a day-by-day journal (日記) but rather scattered thoughts set down in writing — ilji (逸志). So it centers less on dates and events than on the flow of intent and feeling.
js_093: Before changing his pen name, he went by Yeonha. The name Baekbeom carries the hope that every Korean, at minimum, would hold as much love of country as he did.
js_094: As a local Donghak leader, Kim Gu led an attack on Haeju’s fortress and was badly defeated. Donghak was both his first community beyond class and his first defeat.
js_095: It happened at an inn in Chihapo, Anak, Hwanghae Province. Kim Gu saw his target as part of the group that had harmed the queen, and stood by that claim even under trial after his capture.
js_096: That the execution was never carried out is confirmed by primary records. But the detail in The Baekbeom Diary about the royal order arriving by telephone is disputed, since phone service between Seoul and Incheon is recorded as starting only afterward.
js_097: Magoksa is a temple still standing in present-day Gongju, and the spot where Kim Gu stayed remains. His time as a monk was brief, but it kept a hunted man alive.
js_098: Chief of Police was the head of the Provisional Government’s security force. Weeding out spies was grim work, but he wrote that it was there he learned to read people.
js_099: It was a time of tightening Japanese surveillance, with money and people both running dry. Kim Gu chose a small band that could make a big impact — that became the Korean Patriotic Corps.
js_100: Yun Bong-gil took an oath photo at a Korean Patriotic Corps ceremony before the act. He was twenty-five, and died in Japan that December.

js_115: Baek from “outcast,” beom from “ordinary person.” A pen name hoping even the lowliest would become masters of their nation.
js_117: Not a day-by-day journal, but scattered thoughts gathered into a record — a will left for his two sons.
js_119: He joined at eighteen and became a local leader the year after. The idea that even outcasts deserved to be treated as human moved the boy.
js_121: The act at Chihapo, carried out under the cause of avenging Empress Myeongseong. Instead of fleeing, he posted his own name.
js_123: The place he asked to serve even as a gatekeeper. From Chief of Police to President — it became his lifelong post.
js_124: An action organization founded in 1931. Both Yi Bong-chang and Yun Bong-gil came out of it.
js_126: A regular army raised in Chongqing in 1940. It aimed for independence won by fighting, not independence handed over.
js_128: Not the most powerful nation, but the most beautiful one — the final answer left in “My Wish.”
js_130: A will left for his two sons, In and Sin
js_131: A father of fifty-three picks up his pen, not knowing when he might die.
js_132: He writes with his two sons, then around ten years old, in mind for the day they’d grow up to read it.
js_133: He states plainly he’ll record not his achievements but his own past faults.
js_134: The first volume was written in Shanghai; the second, over a decade later, in Chongqing.
js_135: What began as a will ends up becoming testimony to an era.
js_137: An Outcast’s Son — Birth, Learning, Donghak
js_138: Born to a poor commoner family in Haeju, Hwanghae Province.
js_139: Studies to become a scholar, hoping to rise, but is crushed by corruption in the state exams.
js_140: Joins Donghak at eighteen and becomes a local leader the following year.
js_141: Leads the attack on Haeju’s fortress, is badly defeated, and becomes a fugitive.
js_142: Takes shelter with An Tae-hun’s family and meets his mentor, Go Neung-seon.
js_143: Writes that he learned the courage to let go of the branch he was clinging to.
js_145: Chihapo and Incheon Prison — A Death-Row Inmate’s Time
js_146: Kills a Japanese man at Chihapo, citing revenge for the queen.
js_147: Instead of fleeing, posts his own name and address and is caught at home.
js_148: Interrogated at the Incheon magistrate’s office and sentenced to death.
js_149: Survives because the king never approves the sentence.
js_150: The prison becomes a school — he reads new books and teaches fellow inmates.
js_151: After nearly two years locked up, he finally breaks out and flees.
js_153: From Monk to Educator — and Back to Prison
js_154: On the run, enters Magoksa and receives the dharma name Wonjong.
js_155: Returns to lay life, encounters Christianity, and throws himself into the new education movement.
js_156: Builds a school in Hwanghae Province and teaches children as a teacher.
js_157: Gets caught up in the Anak Incident and is jailed again for a long stretch.
js_158: In this prison, changes his pen name to Baekbeom and the characters of his given name.
js_159: After release, works a farm while waiting for his moment.
js_161: The Shanghai Provisional Government — Volunteering as a Gatekeeper
js_162: After the March 1st Movement, crosses the Yalu River and flees to Shanghai.
js_163: Famously asks to be made even a gatekeeper for the government building.
js_164: Takes on the role of Chief of Police, weeding out spies and turncoats.
js_165: Endures years when money and people alike drained away, leaving the government little more than a name.
js_166: Writes to Korean immigrants abroad and uses the funds raised to prepare for what comes next.
js_167: From the lowest position comes the biggest resolve.
js_169: The Korean Patriotic Corps and Liberation Army — From Bombs to an Army
js_170: Founds the Korean Patriotic Corps in 1931 and takes direct action.
js_171: Yi Bong-chang throws a bomb at the emperor’s procession in Tokyo.
js_172: Yun Bong-gil throws a bomb onto the stage at Hongkou Park, Shanghai.
js_173: With a bounty on his head, he’s hunted while drifting between Jiaxing and Nanjing.
js_174: In September 1940, holds the founding ceremony of the Korean Liberation Army in Chongqing.
js_175: Independence comes, but he has to return home as a private citizen.
js_178: Asked what he wishes for, he answers “independence” three times running.
js_179: States flatly that without full, independent sovereignty, there’s no individual happiness either.
js_180: Declares he’ll place no ideology above the nation.
js_181: Wishes not for the most powerful nation, but the most beautiful one.
js_182: Finds the foundation of that beauty not in military force, but in the power of culture.
js_183: The point where The Baekbeom Diary stops being a memoir and becomes a declaration.
js_184: The Man Who Posted His Name Instead of Fleeing
js_185: After killing a Japanese man at Chihapo in the spring of 1896, Kim Gu didn’t hide — he walked out having posted his own name and address. Three months later he was caught at home and dragged to the Incheon magistrate’s office; the Justice Ministry sent up an order for hanging, but the king never approved it, sparing his life. Even through three rounds of interrogation, he never backed off from saying he’d avenged the queen.
js_186: The most expensive way to prove you have nothing to hide is to put your own name on it. Could I put my name on my own judgment?
js_187: The Man Who Volunteered as a Gatekeeper
js_188: On reaching Shanghai, he asked to be made even a gatekeeper for the Provisional Government’s building. It was a way of keeping the vow he’d made in prison, sweeping the yard, to become the lowest servant of his country. That request wasn’t granted outright — he became Chief of Police instead — but he stayed on even after everyone else had left, and eventually became President of that same government.
js_189: The one who volunteers for the lowest seat is the one who lasts longest. What am I putting off right now because I think it’s beneath me?
js_190: A Beautiful Nation Instead of a Powerful One
js_191: Asked what the newly freed nation should become, he answered that he had no wish for it to be the most powerful nation on earth. Military force, he wrote, only needed to be enough to stop invasion — the one thing he wanted without limit was the power of culture. It was an answer that came from an era that measured national strength only in military terms.
js_192: What a community holds as its highest value defines its character. What does the place I belong to prize above all else?
js_193: What kind of nation, what kind of community, do I want to live in?
js_194: Baekbeom chose the most beautiful nation over the most powerful one. Write, in one sentence, what you wish the place you belong to would become known for.
js_195: If I started from the lowest seat, what would I do first?
js_196: He asked to be even a gatekeeper, and ended up becoming master of that house. Pick one task in your current position that looks the most beneath you.
js_197: How far should I trust one person’s memoir?
js_198: Written from memory, this book’s dates and details sometimes clash with other records. Set your own standards for when to trust testimony and when to question it.
